reading.text: For many years, people thought that outgoing people made the best leaders. However, researchers have been studying personality for decades, and their results show something different. Many quiet people, often called introverts, are thoughtful and sensible. They listen carefully, think before they speak, and rarely make impulsive decisions. In meetings, they may not talk much, but when they do, their ideas are usually well prepared. Introverts also tend to be good at working alone and concentrating for long periods. Of course, they need time to rest after spending a day with lots of people. Experts say that the best teams have a mix of personalities. Outgoing people bring energy and enthusiasm, while quiet people bring careful thinking. So if you are a quiet person, don't try to change your character. Just be yourself.

reading.text: In many Iraqi families, three generations still live under one roof. Mustafa, who is 17, shares a house with his parents and his elderly grandparents. "There's definitely a generation gap," he laughs. "My grandfather has been reading the same newspaper every morning for fifty years, and I read the news on my phone." But Mustafa believes that living together has defined his character. His grandmother has taught him patience, and his grandfather has told him stories about his upbringing in a village near Hilla. Of course, there are difficulties. The house can be noisy, and it's not easy to find a quiet place to study. However, Mustafa says the family has learnt to cope. "When someone has a problem, we all help. I don't think I could live alone, even after I come of age."

reading.text: Last winter, Noor was looking for something to read in her grandfather's old bookcase. She picked a dusty novel and, as she opened it, a yellow envelope fell out. Inside was a letter dated 1979. Noor's grandfather had written it to her grandmother before they got married, but he had never sent it. By the time Noor finished reading, she had tears in her eyes. In the letter, her grandfather described the first time he had seen her grandmother at a bookshop on Al-Rasheed Street. Noor showed the letter to her grandmother, who was now 84. At first, she didn't say anything. Then she smiled and said, "So that's why he always went to that bookshop!" It was a beautiful coincidence. A letter that had waited forty years finally reached the person it was written for.

reading.text: In the past, many cafés in Baghdad had a storyteller, called a "hakawati". Every evening, while men were drinking tea and playing dominoes, the hakawati sat on a high chair and began his story. He usually told legends and adventures of brave heroes. At the most exciting moment, just as the hero was fighting the villain, the storyteller would suddenly stop and say, "We'll continue tomorrow." The audience always came back the next day because they couldn't stand the suspense! Today, this tradition has almost disappeared. Television and phones have replaced it. However, a few young people in Iraq have started telling stories again in cultural centres and online. They believe that stories teach us morals and bring people together. As one young storyteller said, "Before there were books, there were storytellers. Stories are how humans remember."

reading.text: Many people believe that it takes 21 days to form a new habit. However, a study at University College London found that the real number is closer to 66 days. Researchers asked 96 people to choose a new healthy habit, such as drinking water after breakfast or going for a walk before dinner. Every day, the participants reported how automatic the behaviour felt. For some people, the habit became automatic after just 18 days. For others, it took more than 200 days. The researchers also discovered something encouraging: missing one day did not ruin the process. What mattered most was being consistent over time. So if you are trying to get used to a new routine, don't worry if you have a bad day. Just start again the next morning. Small actions, repeated regularly, slowly change who you are.

reading.en: A Letter to My Future Self
reading.text: At the start of every year, Sara writes a letter to herself and opens it twelve months later. This is part of the letter she wrote last January: "Dear Sara, by the time you read this, you will have finished your first year at medical college. I hope you will have made some good friends, and I hope you won't have given up on your dream. Right now, you are probably worried about exams. Don't be! This time next year, you will be laughing about it. Remember your long-term goal: to become a children's doctor and open a clinic in your village. It isn't easy, but it is achievable if you stay consistent. Work hard, sleep well, and call Mum more often." Sara says the letters help her stay on track. "When I open them, I can see how much I've grown. Sometimes I've achieved more than I expected, and sometimes less. But I always learn something."

reading.text: Most of us spent years at school, but very few teachers taught us how to learn. Scientists who study the brain have discovered a few simple methods that work for almost everyone. The first is "active recall". Instead of reading your notes again and again, close the book and try to remember what you have learnt. This is harder, but it makes memories much stronger. The second is "spaced repetition": review new information after one day, then three days, then a week. The third method is teaching. When you explain an idea to someone else, you quickly notice what you haven't grasped. Finally, sleep is essential. During sleep, the brain organises the information you absorbed during the day. Students who stay up all night before an exam often remember less, not more. So, the next time you hit the books, study smarter, not just harder.

reading.text: Many people think sleep is a waste of time, but doctors disagree. When you sleep, your body repairs muscles, your immune system becomes stronger, and your brain stores the information you learnt during the day. If adults sleep less than six hours a night for a long time, they are more likely to suffer from chronic diseases such as heart problems. Lack of sleep can also cause fatigue, stress and poor concentration. So how can you sleep better? Experts suggest a few simple rules. Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, even at weekends. Avoid coffee after 4 p.m. Keep your bedroom dark and cool, and put your phone away an hour before bedtime, because the light from screens tells your brain that it is still daytime. If you still suffer from insomnia after trying these tips, you should see a specialist.

It includes lots of vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains, fish and olive oil, but very little red meat, sugar or processed food. Interestingly, many traditional Iraqi dishes are similar. Lentil soup, vegetable stews, fresh herbs and dates are all nutritious and full of fibre. The problem is that modern life has changed what we eat. Many families now consume fast food several times a week, and children often drink sugary drinks instead of water. Experts say that if we returned to our grandparents' way of eating, we would be much healthier. They also suggest eating slowly and sharing meals with family. reading.text: In 2010, two friends from Karbala, Haider and Mahdi, both finished school with excellent grades. Haider opted to study medicine in Baghdad, like his father. Mahdi, however, made a spontaneous decision: he turned down a place at university and opened a small mobile phone repair shop. Everyone thought it was a foolish gamble. "If I had listened to my family," Mahdi says today, "I would have become an engineer and I probably would have been happy. But I wouldn't have built my own business." Today, Mahdi owns three shops and employs twelve people. Haider is now a successful surgeon. Both of them believe they made the right choice. "There is no perfect decision," Haider says. reading.text: An Australian nurse named Bronnie Ware spent many years caring for elderly patients in the last weeks of their lives. She often asked them about their regrets, and she noticed that the same ones came up again and again. Later, she wrote a famous book about them. The most common regret was: "I wish I had lived the life I wanted, not the life others expected of me." Many patients had made sacrifices to please their families and had never fulfilled their own dreams. The second was: "I wish I hadn't worked so hard." Many of them felt they had missed their children's childhood. Others said, "I wish I had stayed in touch with my friends," because they had lost touch with people they loved. Finally, many said, "I wish I had let myself be happier." With hindsight, they realised that happiness is partly a choice. The lesson is simple: we cannot undo the past, but we can still change the future.

reading.en: The Ship with No One on Board
reading.text: In December 1872, sailors on a British ship saw another ship moving strangely in the Atlantic Ocean. It was the Mary Celeste, an American ship that had left New York a month earlier. When they climbed on board, they found something bizarre: there was nobody there. The ten people on board, including the captain, his wife and their two-year-old daughter, had vanished. The lifeboat was missing, but there was still plenty of food and water, and the passengers' belongings were untouched. So what happened? Pirates can't have attacked the ship, because nothing valuable was taken. Some people believed in supernatural theories, but most historians are sceptical. One popular theory is that the cargo, which was alcohol, might have leaked and given off dangerous fumes. The captain must have feared an explosion, so he may have ordered everyone into the lifeboat. Sadly, the lifeboat could have sunk in a storm. Nobody has ever found it, and the mystery remains unexplained.

reading.text: Imagine a job where you only have to work four days a week, but you still get the same pay. In 2022, around sixty companies in Britain tried this idea for six months. Employees didn't have to work longer hours on the other days; they simply had to finish the same workload in less time. To make this possible, many companies changed their policies. Some reduced the number of meetings, and others told staff they mustn't send emails after work. The results surprised many experts. Most employees said they felt less stressed and had more time for their families. Fewer people called in sick, and fewer resigned. Most of the companies decided to continue with the four-day week after the experiment ended. However, the system doesn't suit every job. Hospitals, for example, have to stay open every day, so doctors and nurses can't simply stop working on Fridays. Experts say companies ought to test the idea carefully before they make it compulsory.

reading.text: Not all mistakes are disasters. Some of the most important inventions in history came from accidents. In 1928, a Scottish scientist named Alexander Fleming went on holiday and left some dishes of bacteria in his laboratory. He should have cleaned them before he left, but he didn't. When he returned, he noticed that a type of mould had grown on one dish and had killed the bacteria around it. That careless moment led to penicillin, the first antibiotic, which has saved millions of lives. Similarly, in the 1940s, an engineer called Percy Spencer was working with radar equipment when the chocolate bar in his pocket melted. Instead of ignoring it, he tried to identify the cause. The result was the microwave oven. Of course, both men could have thrown their "failures" away. Instead, they asked questions. The lesson? When something goes wrong, don't just blame yourself. Analyse the problem, and it might turn out to be a blessing in disguise.

reading.text: The first call from a mobile phone was made in New York in 1973 by an engineer called Martin Cooper. Interestingly, he called a competitor to tell him the news! The phone he used was a prototype that weighed more than a kilogram, and its battery lasted only about half an hour. Ten years later, the first mobile phone was sold to the public. It cost nearly $4,000, so it was bought mostly by rich business people. In 1992, the first text message was sent. It said simply "Merry Christmas". Then, in the early 2000s, cameras and faster internet were added to phones, and the smartphone was born. Today, billions of smartphones are used around the world, and most of them are manufactured in Asia. Your phone is thousands of times more powerful than the computers that were used to send astronauts to the Moon in 1969. reading.text: In the year 762, the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur chose a place on the River Tigris for his new capital. It was called Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace, but today we know it as Baghdad. The city was designed as a perfect circle, which was very unusual at the time. It was protected by thick walls, and it could be entered through four gates, which were named after the places they faced, such as Kufa and Basra. It is said that around 100,000 workers were employed to build it. In the centre, the caliph's palace and the great mosque were built. Within a few decades, Baghdad had become one of the largest cities in the world. Sadly, nothing of the Round City can be seen today; it was destroyed and rebuilt many times over the centuries. However, its story is still told, and models of it have been made by historians. Today, Baghdad is a densely populated city of millions, and new bridges and buildings are being built every year.

reading.text: Twenty years ago, if you wanted to get your clothes cleaned or your dinner delivered, you had to go out or make several phone calls. Today, almost everything can be done with an app. In many cities, people get their groceries delivered to their door, have their cars washed while they're at work, and even have their pets taken for a walk. Customers can compare quotes, read reviews and pay online in seconds. For busy people, this is very handy. Many young people have also found jobs as couriers, drivers or technicians through these apps. However, not everyone is happy. Some workers complain that they are paid very little and have no guarantee of regular work. Small local shops also find it hard to compete. And some experts worry that we are becoming lazy: "Why learn to fix things when you can get everything done for you?" one sociologist asked. Perhaps the best approach is a balance: use the apps when you need them, but don't forget your local carpenter or tailor.

reading.text: During a hurricane a few years ago, a photo of a shark swimming on a flooded motorway went viral. Thousands of people shared it, and some TV channels even reported it. Later, experts revealed that the photo was fake: someone had added the shark with a computer. Stories like this are everywhere, and researchers have found that false stories often spread faster than true ones online. So how can you protect yourself? First, check the source. Is it a credible news organisation, or a website you have never heard of? Second, look beyond the headline. Sensational headlines are often clickbait, and the article may say something different. Third, check the date; old stories are often shared as if they were new. Fourth, look for the same story on other trusted websites. If no one else is reporting it, be careful. Finally, ask yourself how the story makes you feel. Fake news is designed to make us angry or afraid, because then we share it without thinking. As one journalist told me, "If a story seems too shocking to be true, it probably is."

reading.text: When Ali applied for a job at a large technology company, he expected the usual questions. The interviewer asked him why he wanted the job and what his strengths were. Then, suddenly, she asked him how many tennis balls could fit inside a bus. Ali paused. He wasn't sure if she was joking. "I asked her whether she wanted an exact number," he remembers, "and she told me not to worry about the number and just to explain how I would find the answer." Many big companies ask questions like this. They want to see if candidates can think on their feet, stay calm and solve problems logically. Other famous examples include "If you were an animal, which one would you be?" and "How would you explain the internet to someone from the year 1800?" Experts say there is no right answer. The important thing is to stay calm, think aloud and put your ideas across clearly. Ali must have done well: two weeks later, he received a job offer.

reading.text: In many cultures, a person's word is worth more than gold. In the past, Arab traders often did business without any written contracts. A handshake and a promise were enough, and a man who went back on his word lost his good name in the market. Today, psychologists say that keeping promises is still one of the most important parts of any relationship. In one study, researchers found that people valued a kept promise more than extra help that they hadn't been promised. When a friend breaks a small promise, such as calling you back, it may not seem serious. However, experts warn that small broken promises slowly destroy trust. So what should you do if you can't keep a promise? First, don't make promises you aren't sure about. Second, if something goes wrong, tell the person as soon as possible. Finally, apologise sincerely and offer to make it up to them. As the old saying goes, "A promise made is a debt unpaid."

reading.text: In southern Iraq, where the Tigris and the Euphrates meet, there is a unique landscape of water, reeds and islands. These are the Mesopotamian Marshes, which some people believe were the location of the Garden of Eden. For thousands of years, they have been home to the Ma'dan, or Marsh Arabs, whose way of life is one of the oldest in the world. Traditionally, they live in houses which are built entirely from reeds, and they travel in long, narrow boats called mashoof. Their main source of income is the water buffalo, which provides milk, cheese and the famous Iraqi breakfast cream, geymar. In the 1990s, most of the marshes were drained, and many inhabitants were forced to leave. However, after 2003, water was allowed to return, and some families came back. In 2016, the marshes were added to UNESCO's World Heritage List. Today, the area faces a new problem: drought, which is caused by climate change and lower river levels. reading.text: Many adults stop having hobbies when they start working. They say they don't have time, or they feel guilty about doing something "useless". However, scientists have found that hobbies are far from useless. Learning a musical instrument, for example, can improve memory and concentration at any age. Studies also suggest that people who have creative hobbies, such as painting, knitting or pottery, feel less stressed, because these activities are absorbing: when you focus on your hands, you stop worrying about your problems. Some doctors even call them therapeutic. Hobbies can help at work, too. Employees who do creative activities in their free time often come up with better ideas. Group hobbies, like playing in a football team or singing in a choir, help us make friends and feel part of a community. So how do you start? Experts suggest choosing something you enjoyed doing as a child. Don't expect to be an expert immediately; everyone is a novice at the beginning. Try doing it for twenty minutes, twice a week. After a few months, you may find that your "useless" hobby has become the most rewarding part of your week.

reading.text: For many people, small talk is the hardest part of any party. You're standing next to someone you've never met, there's an awkward silence, and you have no idea what to say. But small talk isn't useless. Experts say that these short, light conversations help us build trust, and they often lead to friendships or even job opportunities. So how can you get better at it? First, start with the situation you're both in: "Lovely weather, isn't it?" or "How do you know the host?" These questions are easy to answer and work as icebreakers. Second, ask open questions that begin with how, what or why, rather than questions that need only a yes or a no. Third, be a good listener. Most people love talking about themselves, so show interest, nod and ask follow-up questions. Fourth, avoid taboo topics, such as salaries, politics or religion, with people you've just met. Finally, remember that everyone feels a little self-conscious, and introverted people often find small talk tiring. The good news is that small talk is a skill, and like any skill, it gets easier with practice.

reading.text: If you live in Iraq, you know dust storms well. The sky turns orange, the sun disappears, and the air becomes so thick that you can hardly see the end of your street. In recent years, these storms have become more frequent and more severe. In 2022, Iraq experienced a series of dust storms that sent thousands of people to hospital with breathing problems and closed airports and schools. Why is this happening? Scientists explain that the main reasons are drought, rising temperatures and the loss of farmland. When the land is too dry, there aren't enough plants to hold the soil in place, so strong winds lift it into the air. Climate change is making summers hotter and rainfall more unpredictable, which makes the problem worse. What can be done? Experts say that planting "green belts" of trees around cities can reduce the dust. Better water management can also help farmers keep their land green. In the meantime, doctors advise people to stay indoors during storms, close their windows and wear a mask if they have to go out.

reading.text: When people think of a holiday in the Middle East, Iraq is not usually the first country that comes to mind. But in recent years, more and more travellers have discovered the country that is often called "the cradle of civilisation". A typical itinerary starts in the north, in Erbil, where visitors climb up to the citadel, one of the oldest continuously inhabited places in the world. Then they travel south to Baghdad. Here, they can take a boat trip on the Tigris, browse the bookshops on Al-Mutanabbi Street and try masgouf, the famous grilled fish. A short drive away is Babylon, which became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019. Many tourists say that walking among the ancient walls is the highlight of the trip. Finally, the most adventurous travellers head to the Marshes in the south, where they sleep in reed houses and explore the waterways by boat. Of course, travelling in Iraq is not always easy. The summer is extremely hot, so the best time to visit is between October and April. But visitors almost always say the same thing: the hospitality of the Iraqi people made it the trip of a lifetime.

reading.text: Twenty years ago, most people bought a few new pieces of clothing every season. Today, many of us buy something new every month, sometimes every week. This is called "fast fashion": cheap, trendy clothes that are produced quickly and sold in huge amounts. It seems like great value for money, but there is a hidden cost. The fashion industry uses a lot of water; making one cotton T-shirt can use around 2,700 litres. Many cheap clothes are made from plastic-based materials, and very few of them are recycled. Most end up in landfill after being worn only a few times. Some experts believe that consumerism and social media are part of the problem: influencers wear an outfit once, and their followers want to copy it. So what can shoppers do? Buying fewer, better-quality clothes is one answer. Second-hand shopping is also becoming popular among young people, and many cities now have clothes-swapping events. Remember: the most sustainable clothes are the ones that are already in your wardrobe.

reading.text: In July 2007, few people expected Iraq to win the Asian Cup. The country was going through a very difficult time, the team couldn't play home matches in Iraq, and their coach, Jorvan Vieira from Brazil, had joined only about two months before the tournament. Other teams, such as Japan, South Korea and Australia, had far bigger budgets and more famous players. Iraq were the underdogs. However, the team played with incredible determination. They finished top of their group, and in the semi-final, after a 0–0 draw, they beat South Korea on penalties. In the final in Jakarta, they faced Saudi Arabia, who had already won the title three times. In the second half, captain Younis Mahmoud scored with a header, and Iraq won 1–0. Back home, millions of people celebrated in the streets. For many Iraqis, it was much more than a football match: the players came from different parts of the country, and the victory showed what people could achieve together. For many fans, the harder life became, the more this team meant to them.

reading.text: Iraq is known as the land between two rivers, but in recent years, it has faced a serious water crisis. Although the Tigris and the Euphrates have supported life in Mesopotamia for thousands of years, their water levels have fallen dramatically. There are several reasons for this. Rising temperatures and lower rainfall mean that more water evaporates and less reaches the rivers. Dams built upstream, outside Iraq, also reduce the amount of water that arrives. In addition, a lot of water is wasted because of old irrigation methods and leaking pipes. The effects are serious: farmers are losing their land, the Marshes are drying up, and some rural families have had to move to cities in order to find work. Despite these problems, there is hope. Experts say that modern irrigation, such as drip systems, can save a large amount of water. Some farmers are already using them so that they can grow more crops with less water. At home, simple steps such as fixing leaks and taking shorter showers can also make a difference. Water is life, and protecting it is everyone's responsibility.

reading.text: How many times a day do you check your phone? Some studies suggest that many people pick it up more than a hundred times a day, often without even noticing. We scroll through social media, reply to group chats, check our inbox and watch videos until late at night. It's no surprise that a growing number of people are trying a "digital detox": a period of time when they turn off their devices completely. Some people do it for one evening a week; others go offline for a whole weekend. Those who try it often report that they sleep better, feel less anxious and get on with their work more easily. Many also say that they communicate better with their families. However, a digital detox isn't always easy. At first, people often feel that they are missing important news, and it can be hard to keep up with friends. Experts suggest starting small. Turn off notifications you don't need, put your phone in another room while you eat, and don't take it to bed. Remember: your phone is a great tool, but it shouldn't be your boss.

reading.text: What makes some people more successful than others? For a long time, many people believed the answer was talent. However, research by psychologists such as Carol Dweck and Angela Duckworth suggests that something else matters just as much. Dweck found that people with a "growth mindset", who believe that their abilities can improve with effort, often achieve more than people with a "fixed mindset", who think that intelligence is something you either have or don't have. Duckworth studied students, military cadets and salespeople, and discovered that "grit", a mix of passion and persistence, was often a better predictor of success than intelligence. In other words, the people who succeed are often the ones who stick with it when things get hard. This is good news for language learners. Nobody is born speaking English; every fluent speaker was once a novice who made mistakes and felt self-conscious. If you have reached Day 30 of this course, you have already shown the grit that matters. The most important lesson is simple: the brain is like a muscle. The more you train it, the stronger it becomes.
